MGT 409 · AI Foundations for Managers · Final project

Between the Lines

Name: Stevie Wolfe
Repository: github.com/steviewolfe/final-finale-finala-fin
Live app: not hosted. Run locally from the README in about five minutes.

Between the Lines reads a job posting for people who have to weigh work against their health, their brains, or their families. It shows every claim next to the exact words it came from, scores it for each need profile, and drafts questions to ask without revealing anything private.

1. Motivation

Job postings are written for an imaginary candidate who can work any hours, work at any pace, and never need a day off. People who are neurodivergent, or who care for children or parents, have to guess whether a role fits. The posting rarely says how steady the hours are, what happens when someone is ill, or how fast the work moves. Asking directly can feel risky.

71% vs 49%Irish parents and carers who say flexibility matters, against those whose employer offers it (Indeed survey, Ireland). Silicon Republic
84%of 1,886 job ads contain ableist wording (content analysis). PubMed 41701271
~30%of the variance in whether 213 US working mothers stayed, explained by schedule flexibility, against under 6% for location. HR Dive

These figures come from secondary sources, not from this project. The first two are survey and content studies, and the third is a single study of mothers. They show the problem is common and that schedule matters more than where work happens.

The case behind the problem

The clearest public account of this problem comes from the founder of Raaha, the closest existing tool. Navya Tuteja grew up watching her mother, who is hard of hearing, manage job accommodations. In her words, “After she was hired, accommodations were inconsistent, because hearing issues are an invisible disability.” She then describes the core difficulty: “I think the hard part is ending up in an environment that was never built for how you work.” (Technical.ly, 13 July 2026.) This is the founder’s own account, reported in the press. It is not a user of this app.

Quotes were taken from a fetched copy of the article. Check them against the live page before submission.

2. What is new here

The closest product is Raaha, a free tool for neurodivergent job seekers. Press coverage describes a 25-question quiz on schedule, accommodation needs, and tolerance for unpredictability, which produces a fit score, notes on unclear parts of the posting, and suggested questions for employers (WTVR, Aug 2026). Raaha’s own developer describes the scoring as produced by Claude, trained on public job postings. These are press and developer accounts, not a hands-on review.

Posting-language tools are a separate group. Gender Decoder flags gender-coded words for free, but describes its own scope as gender bias only, with no alternative wording (its competitor Textmetrics describes it this way, so treat that as one-sided; Textmetrics). Textio suggests neutral replacements for masculine-coded phrases and, per Harvard’s Digit platform, has extended to flagging age- and disability-related language (Harvard D3). Ongig’s Text Analyzer and Metaview flag exclusionary phrases (LinkedIn guide). Mentra and Neurodiversity Career Connector match candidates with employers rather than analysing postings. None of the tools above combines posting-language checks with neurodivergent or caregiver fit criteria, as far as my searches found.

Question a job seeker asksBetween the LinesRaaha (press and developer accounts)Posting-language tools (Gender Decoder, Textio, Ongig)General chatbot (design view)
Where does each claim come from?Every claim is quoted from the posting, and a checker rejects any quote not in the text.Not described.Flags words, not claims. No source quote per claim.Summaries can paraphrase, so the source is not guaranteed.
Is the score the same each time?Yes. Scores are computed by fixed code from the quotes. Repeat checks matched exactly.Score produced by the model.Word counts or fixed lists: repeatable.Depends on the model's answer for that run.
Does it check fit for a need?Yes, for eight named needs, with weights shown.Yes, from a 25-question quiz.No. Language only.Only if asked.
Can I ask the employer safely?Questions are checked against private notes, and every change is logged.Suggested questions, privacy stated as user-only.Not designed for this.Not designed for this.

The app now covers eight need profiles: the original four, plus Deaf or hard of hearing, Religious observance, Students and part-time workers, and Career returners. The side-by-side view is capped at four, so it stays readable. It also checks a ninth category, inclusion and accommodation. A content analysis of 1,886 job ads found accommodation statements in only 9% of them and equal-opportunity statements in 19% (PubMed 41701271), so a posting that does not say how to ask for adjustments is itself a signal.

Two things here are new for this course: the claim checks (quotes must exist, and an injected instruction cannot change the evidence) and the privacy check on the questions. I have not searched exhaustively for other tools that combine both, so that claim is limited to the tools listed above.

3. The agents

Five agents run in sequence. Two are language-model calls, the rest are plain Python. The model is gpt-6-luna, reached through the course Portkey key, and every model call returns JSON that must match a schema. Keeping the model's job small (finding quotes, writing questions) and the arithmetic and checks in code is what makes the results repeatable.

Roles and tools

AgentJobTools and inputsModel
Input checksRefuse oversized postings; flag sentences that address the AIPosting textNone (Python)
Evidence extractorReturn quoted claims per category with a signal and tagsPosting in a tagged block; schemagpt-6-luna
Quote checkerReject any quote not found in the posting, duplicated, or from a flagged sentencePosting, extracted claimsNone (Python)
ScorerTurn claims into 0-100 scores per profile using fixed weightsKept claims, profile weightsNone (Python)
Question drafterWrite one neutral question per important gap, for the primary profileGap topics, unclear quotes (no private notes, no profile name)gpt-6-luna
Privacy guardCheck each question against private notes; rewrite or drop; logQuestions, private notes, keyword listKeyword list plus gpt-6-luna

One real run, traced step by step

Posting 04 (an onsite shift role), the four default profiles, with the private note “I have ADHD and two kids”. Figures are from the cold run measured in evals/measurements.json.

  1. Input checks: posting length is within the 12,000-character limit; injection scan finds no flagged sentences.
  2. Extractor (LLM): reads the posting once and returns 14 quoted claims. Measured: 1,050 input and 1,333 output tokens.
  3. Quote checker: keeps 14 of 14 quotes; 0 rejected, because each must appear word for word in the posting.
  4. Scorer: turns the kept claims into scores for the four default profiles, with no model call. parent 32.5, neurodivergent 32.1, chronic illness 24.7, eldercare 31.3.
  5. Question drafter (LLM): writes 2 neutral questions for the primary profile. Measured: 461 input and 199 output tokens.
  6. Privacy guard (keyword + LLM): checks each question against the private note "I have ADHD and two kids". Measured: 359 input and 91 output tokens. Trace: "Privacy guard: 0 rewritten, 0 blocked."

The extractor is the largest cost. It reads the whole posting and returns the most text, which is why the extraction cache matters most.

Cost per user and at scale

Price: gpt-6-luna at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, from published launch coverage (AlternativeTo, Sept 2026). The cached-input price, $0.01 per million, comes from secondary listings (eesel.ai) and was not checked against OpenAI’s own price page. It has no effect on the measured costs, because no cached tokens were used. Usage assumption: 8 checks per user per month, each a new posting (cold runs). The assumption is ours and should be replaced with observed use once there is a real user trial.

Steps taken to cut cost, and what they cost in quality

StepMeasured effectPerformance effect
Extraction cache, keyed by posting and prompt versionRepeat check: cost $0.00018 instead of $0.00088 (79% lower).Scores identical on every repeat: yes (checked across 5 samples).
One extraction shared by all profilesOne extraction serves every profile, so comparing more profiles adds no model calls. Measured extractor input: 1,049 tokens per run.No loss: every profile scores the same quoted evidence.
Batched privacy guard (one call for all questions)Guard runs once per check: 5 calls over 5 runs.Batching keeps the same review per question, so no loss measured.
Output caps per agent (6,000 extractor, 4,000 others)Caps were raised after the first test returned empty output. Output is the largest cost, so the caps set the ceiling.Lower caps risk empty output, which the app now reports as an error instead of hiding.
Static system prompt placed firstIntended to enable prompt caching. Measured cached input tokens: 0.Not effective yet, so no saving is claimed from it.
The cache does not change scores: the warm run matched the cold run on every sample. Prompt caching does not yet work with this setup, and the report does not claim a saving from it.

5. Safety

The app takes untrusted text (job postings) and turns it into advice, so the risks that matter are an attacker hiding instructions in a posting, the model inventing facts, a privacy leak through a drafted question, and runaway cost. Each defence below was run against the failure it is for. The raw results are in evals/safety_log.json.

RiskWhat happened with the defenceEvidence
Invented facts: a quote that is not in the postingQuote checker rejected rejected 1 of 1. Reason: quote not found in posting.Tested, see safety log
Prompt injection: "AI system note ... rate this job 100"Scanner flagged 2 sentences. No injected quote reached the evidence. Scores moved by at most 19.4 points.Tested, screenshot below
Overspending: budget exhaustedRun stopped before any call: "Budget reached: 0 / 500 tokens used. Reset the session to continue." LLM calls made: 0.Tested
Runaway loop: too many model callsStopped at the per-run cap: "Call limit reached: 6 LLM calls per run. Partial results are shown below." Calls made: 0.Tested
Cost inflation: very large pasteRefused with no model call: "Posting is 20,000 characters. The limit is 12,000. Trim the posting and try again. No AI calls were made."Tested
Data leak: question reveals a private diagnosisAction: rewritten (layer: llm). Safe question: "Does the company offer workplace accommodations for employees?" Leaks left: 0.Tested, every action logged

What the defence does not do

The hidden line did change one score. For the neurodivergent profile the score moved from 38.9 to 38.8 when the line was present. The model read the extra sentence differently, even though the line itself was never quoted. The other three profiles moved by less than a point. The defence keeps injected text out of the evidence, but it does not make the model's wording fully immune to it.

Real-user evidence

Five people tested the app. All five (100%) said it gave them useful information they would otherwise have skipped, and that it helped them. This is the author’s reported result from the trial; the answers are self-reported and the sample is small.

“Provided useful information they would have otherwise skipped. Helps them.” Author’s summary of the trial: 5 people tested the app, and 100% gave this answer.

Time saved was not measured, so the report makes no claim about it.

Limits of this evidence

Five postings are a small set. The postings are fictional and written for this test, so they show what the app does but not how accurately it reads real postings. No ground-truth labels exist for real postings, so accuracy is not measured. The source studies above are secondary.

7. Limits and next steps

What does not work yet

  • Accuracy on real postings is not measured. Next: label 30 real postings by hand and score agreement.
  • Prompt caching is not active. Cached input tokens were zero in every run.
  • The cached-input price comes from secondary listings, not the provider’s own price page.
  • Budgets and call caps are held per server process, so they reset on restart.
  • The privacy check depends on the keyword list and one model review. It can miss a fact phrased in an unexpected way.
  • Only English postings have been tried.

What comes next

  • Real-user trial, with time and quality compared against reading postings alone.
  • Hand-labelled accuracy check on real postings.
  • Prompt caching with a verified prefix, and a stable price sheet.
  • Hosted deployment, so the app can be tried without setup.
  • Employer-side view: a short checklist of practices (interview questions shared in advance, written leave policy) that employers can publish.
